validated_results.title: Dietary Fatty Acids and Bladder Cancer Risk: Insights from the PLCO Cancer Screening Trial.
validated_results.reason: Prospective PLCO cohort analysis reporting dietary monounsaturated fatty acid intake and incident bladder cancer risk with a gender-specific hazard ratio.

extraction.comparison_type: Higher vs lower dietary MUFA intake (highest vs lowest category), women
extraction.population: Participants of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial

sample_size.excerpt: A quantitative analysis was conducted using data from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial, which included 101,731 participants.

cases.excerpt: During a median follow-up of 11.3 years, 861 bladder cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P-trend = 0.028). However, restricted cubic spline analysis revealed no linear relationship between MUFA intake and bladder cancer risk in the overall group or gender-specific subgroups.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P-trend = 0.028).

comparison.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females

design.excerpt: The Cox proportional hazards model was used to calculate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for bladder cancer risk

timing.excerpt: During a median follow-up of 11.3 years, 861 bladder cancer cases were identified.

continent.excerpt: Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial

exposure_measurement.excerpt: the relationship between the consumption of different dietary fatty acids and the risk of bladder cancer

gender.excerpt: reduced risk of bladder cancer in females

validated_results.title: Adherence to the EAT-Lancet diet reduces the risk of renal cancer: Results from a population-based prospective study.
validated_results.reason: Population-based prospective PLCO cohort study reporting adherence to the EAT-Lancet (planetary health) diet and incident renal cancer risk with an adjusted hazard ratio.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest vs lowest quartile of EAT-Lancet diet adherence
extraction.population: American adults in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial

sample_size.excerpt: A population-based prospective study of 101,755 American adults from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial.

cases.excerpt: Over 899,337.5 person-years of follow-up, 446 cases of renal cancer were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: In the fully adjusted model, a significant inverse association was observed between higher ELD adherence and renal cancer risk (HR for highest vs. lowest quartile: 0.65; 95 % CI: 0.49-0.88; P for trend = 0.002).
